title: Doctors' association sells its tobacco shares
what: The American Medical Association sold about 1.4 million dollars of shares in R.J. Reynolds and Philip Morris from its pension fund. Medical students and young doctors had called it contradictory for a medical group to profit from cigarette makers; a spokeswoman said the publicity had hurt.
why: An early sign of the stigma that would follow tobacco shares, and of the 'sin stock' discount that kept their valuations low and their dividend yields high.

title: Philip Morris opens a giant cigarette plant in North Carolina
what: Philip Morris began production on 3 January at a new 260 million dollar plant in Concord, North Carolina, with 1.8 million square feet. It starts with 350 workers on one shift and is to employ 2,500 and make about 60 billion cigarettes a year by 1986. More than 32,000 people have shown interest in the jobs, which pay about 9 dollars an hour.
why: The company was still investing heavily in a shrinking US market because Marlboro kept taking share.

title: 'Call for Philip Morris': the bellhop goes to the Smithsonian
what: The red uniform of 'Johnny', the tiny bellhop who shouted 'Call for Philip Morris' on radio and television for 25 years, is to go on show at the Smithsonian's Museum of American History in November. Albert Altieri was hired in 1935 and retired in 1982 after 47 years with the company.
why: A reminder of how old and how marketing-driven the business is; the Marlboro Man had long replaced Johnny.

title: Philip Morris completes the 5.75 billion dollar purchase of General Foods
what: Philip Morris completed its takeover of General Foods, the maker of Maxwell House coffee, Jell-O and Kool-Aid, which it agreed in late September at 120 dollars a share, 5.75 billion dollars in all. It is the biggest takeover outside the oil industry so far and creates the largest consumer products company in the United States. This year Philip Morris is also passing Reynolds as the biggest US cigarette maker.
why: The start of the food diversification financed by cigarette cash. It later took two spin-offs (Kraft in 2007, PMI in 2008) to undo the conglomerate.

title: Philip Morris falls 22% in the crash
what: Philip Morris shares lost about 22% in October, as much as the whole market, in the worldwide crash of 19 October. The shares had risen strongly this year.
why: A market move that wiped out the gains of August; the business kept growing and the shares were back above their September 1987 level by mid-1989.

title: Philip Morris buys Kraft for 13.1 billion dollars
what: On 30 October Kraft agreed to be bought by Philip Morris for 106 dollars a share, about 13.1 billion dollars, after Philip Morris raised its hostile offer from 90 dollars. It is the second-largest takeover in US history and makes Philip Morris the world's largest consumer goods company, with Kraft cheese, Philadelphia cream cheese and Velveeta next to General Foods' brands.
why: Food became more than half the group's revenue, but cigarettes stayed most of the profit; Kraft and General Foods were merged into Kraft General Foods.

title: Four-for-one split and a 22% higher dividend
what: Philip Morris's board approved a four-for-one stock split and raised the quarterly dividend 22%, to 1.375 dollars a share before the split. The shares closed at 163.50 dollars. The company earned 1.34 billion dollars in the first half, on revenue of 22.4 billion against 15.4 billion a year earlier, thanks to Kraft.
why: The late 1980s were the stock's golden years: from the end of 1985 to the end of 1991 the share price rose about sevenfold.

title: Philip Morris adds Jacobs Suchard to its food empire
what: This year Philip Morris bought Jacobs Suchard, the Swiss coffee and chocolate maker, for 4.1 billion dollars, and combined General Foods and Kraft into Kraft General Foods, the world's second-largest food company. Food now brings in more than half of the group's revenue, but cigarettes still earn most of the profit.
why: The high point of the conglomerate; it took until 2007 to separate food from tobacco again.
source: https://www.referenceforbusiness.com/history2/72/Philip-Morris-Companies-Inc.html (read 2026-10-03; the month of the Jacobs Suchard purchase is not given there); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Foods (read 2026-10-03)

title: Rate cut lifts the market; Philip Morris up 18%
what: The Federal Reserve cut its discount rate by a full point to 3.5% in December and stocks surged; Philip Morris gained about 18% in the month, ending the year near its record. Michael Miles, the former head of Kraft and the first non-smoker to lead a major tobacco company, took over as chairman and chief executive this year from Hamish Maxwell, who built the food business.
why: The top of the first great run: by April 1993, after 'Marlboro Friday', the shares were about 40% lower.

title: 'Marlboro Friday': Philip Morris cuts the price of Marlboro
what: On Friday 2 April Philip Morris announced a 20% price cut for Marlboro to win back smokers who are switching to cheap generic cigarettes. Its shares fell 26% that day, and other brand-name consumer companies such as Coca-Cola and RJR Nabisco fell too. Investors fear that brands no longer allow premium prices.
why: The defining shock of the 1990s for the stock (-27% in the month). The fear proved wrong: Marlboro regained share and prices rose again, but it was a reminder that the cash machine could break.

title: Tobacco bosses tell Congress nicotine is not addictive
what: On 14 April the chief executives of the seven largest US tobacco companies, including Philip Morris, testified under oath before a House subcommittee chaired by Henry Waxman that they did not believe nicotine is addictive.
why: The images of the seven executives became a symbol of the industry's denial and fuelled the lawsuits by states and smokers that followed.

title: Liggett breaks ranks and settles
what: In March the small cigarette maker Liggett, with about 2% of the US market, agreed to settle smoking-and-health lawsuits, the first company to do so. Philip Morris and the other big makers say they will not settle and will fight every case. At the end of 1995 there were 125 smoking-and-health cases pending against Philip Morris, 88 of them filed in Florida since April 1995, and several states are suing to recover Medicaid costs. Geoffrey Bible is chairman and chief executive.
why: The start of the legal avalanche that ended in the 1998 Master Settlement; the shares fell 11% in March 1996.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764180/0000950146-96-000483.txt (Philip Morris 10-K for 1995, filed March 1996, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liggett_Group (read 2026-10-03); month change from data/out/mo.json

title: Tobacco industry offers a 368.5 billion dollar national settlement
what: On 20 June state attorneys general and the big tobacco companies announced the outline of a national settlement: the companies would pay 368.5 billion dollars over 25 years, accept possible regulation by the Food and Drug Administration and limits on marketing, and in return get protection from class actions. It needs the approval of Congress.
why: Congress never passed it; the industry settled with the states separately in 1998 on cheaper terms.

title: The Master Settlement: 206 billion dollars to the states
what: On 23 November the four largest US cigarette makers, Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds, Brown & Williamson and Lorillard, signed the Master Settlement Agreement with 46 states and several territories. They will pay at least 206 billion dollars over the first 25 years and accept limits on marketing; in return the states drop their claims for smoking-related health costs.
why: The industry passed the cost on through higher prices and stayed hugely profitable, but the settlement did not stop lawsuits by individual smokers, which dominated 1999 to 2003.

title: Florida court revives a giant smokers' class action: bankruptcy fears
what: In July a Miami jury in the Engle class action found the tobacco companies liable to Florida's sick smokers, estimated at 500,000 to a million people. In October a panel of three appeals judges ruled that punitive damages must be decided in one lump sum for the whole class, and analysts say they could exceed 300 billion dollars. Philip Morris shares fell to about 21 dollars, down almost 40% since August; experts say bankruptcy of the tobacco companies is a real possibility. This year Philip Morris began saying on its website, for the first time, that smoking can cause lung cancer and other diseases.
why: The worst stretch of the stock: -64% from November 1998 to February 2000. It also emerged that company insiders, including CEO Geoffrey Bible, had sold shares in August.

title: Florida caps the Engle bond; Philip Morris eyes Nabisco: tobacco shares rally
what: In early May the Florida legislature passed a bill that spares cigarette makers most of the risk of having to post a bond worth billions of dollars to appeal a verdict in the Engle class action, which could have bankrupted them. Philip Morris is also reported to be the frontrunner in the bidding for Nabisco. Philip Morris shares gained about 19% in May; analysts say investors think the worst is behind the companies.
why: The turning point after the 1999 panic: from February 2000 to February 2001 the shares gained 139%, their best twelve months in the game.
source: https://www.wired.com/2000/05/holy-smoke-tobacco-boosts-dow/ (Reuters report of 15 May 2000, read 2026-10-03); move from data/out/mo.json

title: Engle jury: 145 billion dollars in punitive damages
what: A Florida jury ordered Philip Morris and four other tobacco companies to pay 145 billion dollars in punitive damages to the class of sick Florida smokers, by far the largest award in US history. Philip Morris's share is nearly 74 billion dollars. The companies will appeal, and under the new Florida law the bond they must post is limited.
why: Thanks to the bond cap the shares fell only about 5% in July; many analysts expected the verdict to be overturned, as it was in 2003.
source: https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2001-feb-02-fi-20218-story.html (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Engle (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Florida (largest punitive award, read 2026-10-03); month change from data/out/mo.json

title: Philip Morris was the best Dow stock of 2000
what: Philip Morris shares gained 90% in 2000, the best performance among the 30 Dow Jones stocks in a year when most indexes fell; at about 46 dollars they are more than twice their level of January 2000. The company earned 8.5 billion dollars in 2000. Investors expect the Engle verdict to be overturned, think the new Bush administration will be gentler on tobacco, and like a business that sells in any economy as technology stocks crash.
why: Explains the rally of 2000, including big monthly gains in October and December 2000 for which no single cause was found.

title: Kraft goes public in the second-largest IPO ever
what: Philip Morris sold about 16% of Kraft Foods to the public in June, raising 8.7 billion dollars in the second-largest initial public offering to date; it keeps 84% of the shares and 98% of the votes. Kraft now includes Nabisco, the maker of Oreo and Ritz, which Philip Morris bought in 2000 for 55 dollars a share in cash, an enterprise value of 18.9 billion dollars. It is the largest food company in North America.
why: Gave the market a price for the food business and prepared the full spin-off of 2007.
source: https://www.referenceforbusiness.com/history2/72/Philip-Morris-Companies-Inc.html (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764180/000095013000003538/0000950130-00-003538-0002.txt (Nabisco terms, Philip Morris 8-K of 26 June 2000, read 2026-10-03)

title: A string of verdicts revives litigation fears
what: On 11 June a Miami jury ordered Philip Morris, Brown & Williamson and Liggett to pay 37.5 million dollars to a former smoker, John Lukacs, a member of the Engle class, and found him entitled to a share of the 145 billion dollar Engle punitive award. On 21 June a federal judge in Kansas ordered R.J. Reynolds to pay 15 million dollars in punitive damages, and the industry has lost five verdicts in a row on the West Coast. On 24 June Philip Morris shares fell 7.3% to 48.80 dollars. They had been among the best blue chips this year. At the end of May Philip Morris agreed to sell Miller Brewing to South African Breweries for 3.6 billion dollars in shares plus 2 billion of debt, keeping 36% of the new SABMiller.
why: The litigation discount returned after the 2000-2001 rally; the shares lost about 24% in June.

title: Philip Morris slashes its profit forecast
what: On 26 September Philip Morris cut its 2002 forecast to earnings growth of 3 to 5%, against about 19% analysts expected. It blamed sharp increases in state cigarette taxes (the average state tax is up 35% since June), consumer frugality, cheap imports and a black market in untaxed and counterfeit cigarettes, against which it is spending more on promotions. The shares fell 12% after hours. Its cigarette market share dipped to 49% in July.
why: The second leg of the 2002 slump; tax increases and the black market, not lawsuits, were this time the problem.

title: Philip Morris Companies becomes Altria
what: The parent company of Philip Morris USA, Philip Morris International and Kraft Foods changed its name to Altria Group in January. The company says the name reflects that it is more than a cigarette maker; critics say it wants to escape the stigma of tobacco.
why: A name change only; the players' holding continues under the new name.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altria (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764180/000095011703000291/ex99.txt (financial statements of Altria Group, formerly Philip Morris Companies, filed 29 January 2003, read 2026-10-03)

title: Illinois 'lights' verdict: 10.1 billion dollars and a 12 billion dollar bond
what: A judge in Madison County, Illinois, ordered Philip Morris USA to pay 10.1 billion dollars in a class action claiming that 'light' cigarettes were sold as less harmful, and to post a 12 billion dollar bond to appeal. The company says it cannot post a bond that large and may be unable to make its 2.6 billion dollar payment to the states due on 15 April. Altria shares lost about 22% in March.
why: The second bankruptcy scare. On 14 April the judge cut the bond to 800 million dollars in cash plus a 6 billion dollar note in escrow, and the company made its payment to the states.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764180/000119312503000925/dex991.htm (Philip Morris USA press release of 14 April 2003, which describes the March order; read 2026-10-03); move from data/out/mo.json

title: Appeals court throws out the 145 billion dollar Engle verdict
what: In May Florida's Third District Court of Appeal overturned the 145 billion dollar Engle verdict. It ruled that the smokers were too different to be treated as one class, that the punitive damages were excessive, and that the plaintiffs' lawyers had used racially charged arguments to prejudice the jury. Altria shares gained about 34% in May, their best month in the game.
why: The end of the existential threat; the stock never again faced a bankruptcy scare and more than doubled by 2007.

title: Altria considers breaking itself up
what: On 4 November chairman Louis Camilleri told investors that Altria's tobacco businesses are significantly undervalued compared with other tobacco companies, and that Altria is looking at separating into two or three independent companies, preparing to act 'when the litigation environment permits'. He expects 2004 earnings at the top of the guided range of 4.55 to 4.60 dollars a share. Altria shares gained about 19% in November.
why: The first public statement of the break-up plan carried out in 2007 and 2008; the link to the November gain is plausible but not confirmed by a source read here.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764180/000115752304010378/a4758835ex99.txt (Altria press release of 4 November 2004, read 2026-10-03); month change from data/out/mo.json

title: Judge finds the tobacco companies guilty of racketeering
what: On 17 August federal judge Gladys Kessler ruled in a 1,683-page opinion that Philip Morris and the other big tobacco companies violated the racketeering (RICO) law by conspiring for decades to deny the health risks and addictiveness of smoking and by marketing to children. She ordered them to stop using terms like 'light' and 'low tar' and to publish corrective statements, but imposed no damages. Earlier this year the Florida Supreme Court decertified the Engle class, ending the 145 billion dollar award for good, but let individual smokers rely on the jury's findings.
why: Morally damning, financially manageable: no payments were ordered. The Engle findings did lead to many individual 'Engle progeny' cases that cost the industry for years.

title: Altria spins off Kraft
what: On 30 March Altria distributed its roughly 89% stake in Kraft Foods to its shareholders, about 0.7 Kraft share for each Altria share. Chairman Louis Camilleri says an independent Kraft can grow faster and make acquisitions with its own shares. Altria keeps the US and international cigarette businesses.
why: In the game's price series the Kraft shares are folded into Altria's price (earlier history scaled down), so a holder sees no jump. The split was decided once the litigation threat had eased.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764180/000119312507017014/dex991.htm (Altria press release of 31 January 2007, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altria (read 2026-10-03)

title: Altria spins off Philip Morris International
what: On 28 March Altria completed the spin-off of Philip Morris International, giving one PMI share for each Altria share. PMI, which sells Marlboro and other brands outside the United States, trades separately from 31 March. Altria keeps Philip Morris USA and is moving its headquarters to Richmond, Virginia.
why: From here Altria is a purely American tobacco company that pays out most of its profit. As with Kraft, the game's price series folds the PMI shares into Altria's price.

title: Altria buys UST, the maker of Copenhagen and Skoal
what: On 8 September Altria agreed to buy UST, the world's leading maker of moist smokeless tobacco (Copenhagen, Skoal), for 69.50 dollars a share in cash, about 11.7 billion dollars including debt. It also gets the Ste. Michelle wine business. Altria expects 250 million dollars of annual savings by 2011.
why: The first big step beyond cigarettes for the new, US-only Altria, completed in 2009 in the middle of the financial crisis.

title: The FDA gets power over tobacco
what: On 22 June President Obama signed the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act, which gives the Food and Drug Administration authority to regulate tobacco products, including their ingredients and marketing.
why: The FDA's power over nicotine and e-cigarettes shaped Altria's fortunes from 2018 on, above all through the Juul ban of 2022.

title: Altria grows earnings despite falling cigarette volumes
what: Altria reported on 27 January that its adjusted earnings per share rose 8.6% in 2010 to 1.90 dollars, helped by higher profits from cigarettes and smokeless tobacco, and announced a new 1 billion dollar share buyback. It expects 6 to 9% earnings growth in 2011.
why: The template of the post-spin-off years: rising prices, cost cuts and buybacks more than offset falling volumes.

title: Barrington succeeds Szymanczyk at Altria
what: Martin Barrington became chairman and chief executive of Altria on 17 May, succeeding Michael Szymanczyk, who retired after 23 years with the company, including four as Altria CEO and 12 as head of Philip Morris USA. Altria pays a quarterly dividend of 41 cents a share.
why: The quiet years: a shrinking cigarette market offset by price increases and buybacks, with the shares rising steadily until 2017.

title: Another year of 7.7% earnings growth
what: Altria reported on 30 January that adjusted earnings per share grew 7.7% in 2013 to 2.38 dollars, with higher prices and brand-building lifting income in all three of its main businesses. It forecasts 6 to 9% growth for 2014.
why: Steady and predictable: the kind of results that made Altria a favourite of income investors.

title: Altria shareholders made 34.5% in 2014
what: Altria reported on 30 January that adjusted earnings per share grew 8.0% in 2014 and that shareholders earned a total return of 34.5%, well above the S&P 500. It raised its dividend for the 48th time in 45 years and launched its MarkTen e-cigarette nationally. Howard Willard becomes chief operating officer and Billy Gifford finance chief in March.
why: The stock was heading for its 2017 peak; e-cigarettes were still a sideline.

title: Altria becomes a big shareholder of AB InBev
what: When Anheuser-Busch InBev completed its takeover of SABMiller on 10 October, Altria received 9.6% of AB InBev and about 5.3 billion dollars in cash for its old Miller stake. Altria expanded its share buyback to 3 billion dollars.
why: Turned the 2002 Miller sale into a stake in the world's biggest brewer.

title: Howard Willard takes over at Altria
what: Howard Willard, a 25-year company veteran who has been chief operating officer and finance chief, succeeded Marty Barrington as chairman and chief executive on 17 May. Altria expects adjusted earnings per share to grow 15 to 19% in 2018, helped by the US tax cut, and raised its share buyback to 2 billion dollars; the quarterly dividend is 70 cents.
why: Willard's tenure (to 2020) is defined by the Juul investment of December 2018.

title: Altria invests 12.8 billion dollars in Juul
what: On 20 December Altria bought 35% of Juul Labs, the leading US e-cigarette maker, for 12.8 billion dollars, valuing Juul at 38 billion. It is the biggest investment in Altria's history; CEO Howard Willard says adult smokers will increasingly choose non-combustible products. Earlier in December Altria agreed to buy 45% of the Canadian cannabis company Cronos for 1.8 billion dollars. Juul is under fire for the popularity of its products among teenagers.
why: The worst deal in the company's history: the stake was written down to a fraction within four years.

title: Altria writes down Juul by 4.5 billion dollars
what: On 31 October Altria wrote down the value of its Juul stake by 4.5 billion dollars, about 35% of what it paid ten months ago. Juul has stopped advertising and replaced its chief executive with an Altria executive amid a crisis over teenage vaping, and the House of Representatives is investigating the Altria deal.
why: The first of several writedowns; by July 2022 the stake was valued at 450 million dollars.

title: Altria sells its wine business
what: On 9 July Altria agreed to sell Ste. Michelle Wine Estates, which it got with UST in 2009, to the private equity firm Sycamore Partners for about 1.2 billion dollars in cash, and plans to use the proceeds for share buybacks. Chief executive Billy Gifford says Altria will focus on moving adult smokers to non-combustible products.
why: Altria back to tobacco only, while it searched for a successor to Juul.

title: FDA orders Juul off the market and targets nicotine
what: On 23 June the Food and Drug Administration ordered Juul to stop selling its e-cigarettes in the United States; an appeals court put the order on hold the next day. Days earlier the FDA said it plans a rule to cap the nicotine in cigarettes at levels that are not addictive, a direct threat to Altria's core business. Altria owns 35% of Juul and has already written much of its value off. Altria shares lost about 23% in June, in a falling market.
why: The low point of the Juul saga; Altria swapped its Juul stake for heated-tobacco patents in March 2023.

title: Altria buys NJOY and gives up Juul
what: On 6 March Altria agreed to buy the e-cigarette maker NJOY for about 2.75 billion dollars in cash, plus up to 500 million depending on regulatory outcomes; NJOY ACE is the only pod-based e-cigarette authorised by the FDA. This month Altria also agreed to exchange its Juul stake for rights to some of Juul's heated-tobacco technology.
why: Altria's reset in smoke-free products under CEO Billy Gifford, after the 12.8 billion dollar Juul loss.

title: Altria sells part of its AB InBev stake to buy back its own shares
what: On 14 March Altria agreed to sell 35 million AB InBev shares in a public offering and to AB InBev for about 2.4 billion dollars, and raised its own share buyback by 2.4 billion dollars. Chief executive Billy Gifford says Altria's shares offer 'significant value' at today's price.
why: Capital returns are the core of the investment case for today's Altria.

title: Altria: the slow-shrinking cash machine
what: Altria reported on 30 October that third-quarter revenue net of excise taxes fell 1.7%, but adjusted earnings per share rose 3.6%; it expects 3.5 to 5% earnings growth for 2025 and expanded its share buyback. In August it raised its dividend for the 60th time in 56 years. Net revenue fell 3% in the quarter as fewer cigarettes are sold.
why: Where the story stands: a high-yield income stock whose total return comes mostly from dividends. The shares fell about 15% in October 2025 for reasons not established here, and were back above 67 dollars by September 2026, still below the 2017 peak.
